news.title: A 'New Plastic Medicare Card' in the Mail Is a Scam
news.excerpt: An official-looking plastic Medicare card is landing in mailboxes, with a phone number to "activate" your new benefits — and that call is the whole scam. Real Medicare cards are paper, and nobody from Medicare will ever call, text, or email asking for your Medicare, Social Security, or bank number. Don't ring a number printed on the letter — type medicare.gov into your browser yourself, or use 800-633-4227, the number I check before I trust it. Already shared it? Report it at ftc.gov.

news.title: If Someone Wants You to Pay With Gift Cards, It's a Scam
news.excerpt: Police put out a fresh warning this week that gift-card scams are going after older adults and draining savings. Here is a rule that never fails: no real bank, sheriff's office, insurance company, or store will ever ask you to pay a bill with gift cards. Once you read the numbers off the back, the money is gone and there is no refund. If a caller keeps you on the line and pushes you to go buy cards, hang up — I've never once seen a real bill that worked that way.

news.title: Microsoft Pulled the Update That Switched Off Word and Excel
news.excerpt: Microsoft pulled a faulty update that switched off Word and Excel on home computers — people opened a document and were told their software was unlicensed, or found it gone. One repair shop had five customers hit within ten minutes, and I've had calls here too. Don't pay to fix it, and be wary of any message offering to do it for you — that's where the scam starts. Open Word or Excel, click Reactivate, and sign in with the account you normally use; if it's gone, reinstall the copy you bought.

news.title: Fake Bill-Pay Ads Are Stealing People's Payments
news.excerpt: Scammers are buying the ads at the top of search results when you look up a bill — power, water, or internet. You click a fake payment page that looks just like your provider's, pay it, and the money goes straight to a crook while your real bill sits unpaid. I check the address bar and type my provider's exact website myself instead of trusting the first ad. Pay only through the bill you were mailed, and report fakes at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

news.title: A Fake 'Free Upgrade' Login Window Wants Your Password
news.excerpt: Scammers are offering a free upgrade to a paid AI tool, then showing a fake Google sign-in window to "claim" it. That window is drawn inside the website — it isn't really Google — so anything you type goes straight to the crooks. A real Google sign-in opens in your browser's own window, never floating inside a page. If one pops up inside a website, close the tab and never type your password. I type google.com myself whenever I'm unsure.

posts.title: Is your email in a data breach? Check free in seconds at haveibeenpwned.com and turn on alerts so a scammer never gets there first
posts.summary: Open haveibeenpwned.com in your browser, type your email address in the box, and click the button. It is free, it takes about ten seconds, and you do not have to create an account or hand over a password. Then scroll down the page and click Notify me, so it sends you an email the day your address shows up in a future leak.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that when a store, a hospital, or an insurance company gets broken into, the list of emails and passwords that gets stolen is often posted for sale where anyone can buy it. Your email address being on that list is not the whole problem — the problem is what a thief does with it next, which is trying your old password on your bank, your Facebook, and your email, because so many people use the same one everywhere. The honest answer is that a leaked email address by itself is not an emergency; a leaked password that you still use is. That is why the check is free and worth ten seconds of your morning.

posts.title: Cannot open a file someone emailed you? 7-Zip is the free file opener at 7-zip.org that unpacks ZIP and RAR files — no account, no ads, nothing to pay
posts.summary: Go to 7-zip.org and click the big Download link for Windows near the top of the page, install it, and you are done. From then on, right-click any ZIP or RAR file and choose 7-Zip, then Extract Here. The contents appear right next to the file, free, forever.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that a zipped file is just a suitcase. It is one file on the outside with a whole folder of files packed inside, and somebody has to unpack it. Windows can open the most common kind — the ZIP — but it cannot touch a RAR, and a RAR is exactly what people send when they are sending a big folder of tax papers, church records, or family pictures. The honest answer is that nothing is wrong with your computer and nothing is wrong with the file — your computer simply does not have the right tool yet. And be careful where you get one: the look-alike openers covered in ads want a monthly fee. The real 7-Zip is a small, quiet piece of software that one programmer has given away free for over twenty years.

posts.title: Stop renting Microsoft Office — LibreOffice is the free office suite at libreoffice.org that opens Word, Excel and PowerPoint files and never sends your documents to AI
posts.summary: Download LibreOffice free from libreoffice.org, install it, and it opens your Word, Excel and PowerPoint files just like the paid versions. There is no subscription, no account, and no AI reading your documents — it works completely on your own computer, even offline.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that the letters, the church newsletter, and the spreadsheet they keep the club's dues in do not require a monthly fee. The bills and cards people get in the mail are almost never for the typing program itself — they are for a subscription that renewed on its own, and the free suite has been doing that same everyday work for years. And here is the part I like best: LibreOffice does not run your documents through somebody else's AI. It doesn't send your writing anywhere, and it doesn't need the internet at all. For a customer typing a letter to the insurance company or a list of medications, that is exactly what you want.

posts.title: Windows 11 Search can finally drop Bing — flip off "web results" free in Settings > Privacy & security > Search
posts.summary: Click Start, open Settings, click Privacy & security, then click Search. Turn off the switch called web results (and, if you like, the one called search highlights). That keeps the little search box focused on your own programs and files instead of fetching ads and web pages every time you type. It is free, it is already built into Windows, and it takes about a minute.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that when the search box on your computer feels slow, it is often not searching your computer at all — it is quietly reaching out to the internet and pulling back web results and advertisements you never asked for. You type "calculator" and it shows you the program, yes, but it also shows you a shopping suggestion and a headline. Starting this September, Windows finally put a plain off switch in the settings for people who just want to find their own stuff. The honest answer is that this will not make a tired old machine new again. But it does make the most-used box on the computer feel calm and private, and it takes one click.

posts.title: Your robot vacuum has a camera — the government just flagged a security flaw in Eufy robot vacuums, so update yours free in the eufy Clean app
posts.summary: Open the free eufy Clean app — the same app you use to start and schedule your vacuum. Tap your vacuum on the screen, tap the three dots in the top right corner, and choose Firmware Update. Before you do, put the vacuum back on its charging base and make sure your home Wi-Fi is steady. It takes a few minutes, it is free, and you do not need to buy anything.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that a robot vacuum is not really a vacuum — it is a small computer on wheels that happens to suck up dust. It runs its own program, it lives on your home Wi-Fi, and the better ones have a camera and a microphone. That is fine, and it is why they work so well — but anything with a camera on your network needs the same care you give your computer. On September 24th our own government's cybersecurity agency warned about this exact model line. It is not a reason to panic or to throw the vacuum away. It is a reason to open the app and press one button. I see this all the time — the device is fine, the owner just did not know it was a computer.

posts.title: Tired of ads following you everywhere? Brave is the free browser at brave.com that blocks them by itself — nothing to add, nothing to pay
posts.summary: Go to brave.com and click the Download button, install it, and then use it exactly like your current browser. Brave blocks ads and the trackers that follow you from site to site on its own, the moment you install it. You do not add anything, you do not change any settings, and you never pay a cent.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that the slow, cluttered feeling on the internet is not your computer wearing out — it is ads. Every news page you open can load a dozen videos and pictures you never asked for, and each of those little ad workers takes a bite out of your machine. But here is the part that actually matters: those same ads are how most people get tricked, because a fake "your antivirus expired" pop-up is usually nothing more than a bad ad on an otherwise ordinary site. The honest answer is that blocking ads is not just about a tidier page — it is one of the simplest safety habits there is.

posts.title: Your family pictures live in one place only — Windows File History keeps an automatic second copy on a $60 portable drive from Walmart; press Start, type File History, and click Turn on
posts.summary: Buy a portable drive — Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba all make good ones, and they run about $60 at Walmart or Best Buy — then plug it into the computer with the cord that comes in the box. Press the Start button, type File History, open it, and click Turn on. From then on, Windows copies your Documents, Pictures, and Desktop onto that drive every hour, by itself, without you clicking anything ever again.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that their pictures live in exactly one place — a spinning metal disc inside the laptop — and that this one piece is both the most likely to fail and the only piece that cannot be ordered new. I can order a screen. I can order a hinge. Aunt Ruth's birthday from 2011 is a different story. The other thing people get wrong is believing that a cloud account is the same as a second copy. The honest answer is that it is not: if a picture gets deleted in the cloud, it is usually deleted everywhere, and there is a monthly bill attached to those limits. An hourly copy that sits on a shelf in your hall closet and needs no internet — that is the real thing.

posts.title: Can't hear the TV or a video on your computer? Windows 11's free Live Captions types out the words — turn it on with Windows key + Ctrl + L
posts.summary: On a Windows 11 computer, press the Windows key, Ctrl, and L at the same time to turn on Live Captions, or open Settings > Accessibility > Captions and flip the Live captions switch. It is free and built in, and it shows on-screen text for any sound your computer plays — a video, a call, or a DVD.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that the biggest reason folks give up on a computer is their ears, not the machine. A customer turns the volume all the way up, the family says it's too loud, and they still miss the words. Meanwhile Windows has had a free feature for years that simply types out whatever is playing, live, right on the screen — and almost nobody turns it on because nobody told them it was there. The honest answer is that this is not only for people with hearing loss. It helps when the speaker is muffled, when a show has a heavy accent, or when you are in a room where you can't turn the sound up. It costs nothing, it is already on the computer, and it lives behind one keyboard shortcut.

posts.title: Windows has free built-in troubleshooters that solve sound, printer, and Wi-Fi problems for you — open Settings > System > Troubleshoot and click Run
posts.summary: Click Start, open Settings, click System, then click Troubleshoot. Under Other troubleshooters, find the problem you are having — no sound, printer not working, Wi-Fi dropping — and click Run next to it. Windows will find the common cause and fix it for you. It is free, it is already on your computer, and nothing to buy or download.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that a huge share of "broken" computers are not broken at all — they are just stuck. A printer that will not print is usually a jammed-up print job, not a dead printer. A Wi-Fi that keeps dropping is usually a tiny setting that got switched, not a dead card. And the tool that fixes most of it has been sitting inside Windows the whole time, free, waiting to be clicked. The honest answer is that people buy a new printer or pay for a mystery "tune-up" service over a problem that a built-in helper fixes in two minutes. I am not against selling you something when you truly need it. I am against selling you something you already own.

posts.title: Firefox now gets a fresh, safer version every two weeks instead of once a month — keep yours current free in Menu, Help, About Firefox
posts.summary: Open Firefox, click the Menu button in the top right corner — it is the three little lines — then click Help, then click About Firefox. A small window opens and Firefox checks for the newest version by itself. If one is waiting it downloads on its own, and you click Restart to update. That is the whole thing: free, no account, about a minute.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize that a web browser is the most-used program on the whole computer. You read the news, check the bank, look at the grandkids' pictures, and pay a bill, all inside one window. Security researchers find holes in browsers constantly, and the makers patch them — which is why, starting this September, Firefox decided to ship a fresh version every two weeks instead of once a month. The browser you are using right now is the front door to everything you do online, and a door that gets its lock changed twice as often is harder to walk through. None of that matters unless you take the update. I see this all the time — a computer that is up to date except for the one program the person uses every single day.
